evidence: The abstract describes experimental results demonstrating this capability.

claim: Protein interactions can be dynamically controlled by post-transcriptional modifications or the presence of small molecules that act as 'molecular glues'.

claim: Splitting the pegRNA into sgRNA and petRNA with complementary RNA sequences as dimerization modules resulted in low editing efficiency (<2%).
source: In general, we observed a low editing efficiency (<2%) by sgRNA-petRNA pairs that are expected to be dimerized by complementary RNA sequences, even with an additional 3' RNA pseudoknot structure that inhibits RNA degradation from 3'-end (Nelson et al., 2022; Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The text describes experimental results shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: A single pegRNA with additional RNA stem-loop structure at the PE-junction exhibited moderate editing efficiency (~10%).
source: The inefficiency in editing is unlikely to be due to the inserted dimerization domain because a single pegRNA with additional RNA stem-loop structure at the PE-junction exhibited moderate editing efficiency (~10%; pegRNA w/ SL condition in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The text describes experimental results shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Editing using pegRNAs containing the self-splicing ribozyme sequence was inefficient (<2%) in all six constructs tested.
source: However, editing using pegRNAs containing the self-splicing ribozyme sequence was inefficient (<2%) in all six constructs.
evidence: The text describes experimental results.

claim: The limited editing observed with self-splicing ribozyme was dependent on ribozyme function.
source: To the limited extent that editing was observed, we found that it was dependent on ribozyme function because including a loss-of-function substitution in the ribozyme sequence reduced editing efficiency by greater than 10-fold (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: The text describes experimental results shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The distal double-stranded RNA region of the crRNA:tracrRNA junction is not necessary for Cas9 function.
source: Previous reports have shown that the distal double-stranded RNA region of the crRNA:tracrRNA junction (also known as the repeat:anti-repeat junction) is not necessary for Cas9 function; this region is replaced by the GAAA tetraloop sequence in the standard sgRNA constructs (Jinek et al., 2012).

claim: Using the 10 bp dimerization sequence found in the standard sgRNA, editing efficiency at HEK3 was 15%, which was 37% of the editing efficiency of the standard epegRNA.
source: Using the 10 bp dimerization sequence found in the standard sgRNA, we observe editing efficiency at HEK3 of 15% (Figure 1d), which was 37% of the editing efficiency of the standard epegRNA programming of the same edit ('eCTT control') with the same PE4max prime editor.
evidence: The text describes experimental results shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Flipping A-U pairs at the bottom of repeat:anti-repeat duplex enhanced editing efficiency to 28%, which is 76% of the editing efficiency of the eCTT control.
source: The editing efficiency was further enhanced to 28% by flipping A-U pairs at the bottom of repeat:anti-repeat duplex, which is 76% of the editing efficiency of the eCTT control.
evidence: The text describes experimental results.

claim: Removing the dimerization sequence reduced the editing efficiency to 2.7%.
source: In contrast, removing the dimerization sequence reduced the editing efficiency to 2.7%, which further reduced to 0.3% when the upper part of the Cas9-binding duplex was removed (Figure 1c and d; short-1 and short-2 designs).
evidence: The text describes experimental results shown in Figure 1c and d.

claim: Pairing crRNA and petracrRNA with unmatching dimerization sequences resulted in low editing efficiency (2–3%).

claim: Splitting the pegRNA at the repeat:anti-repeat portion is the most promising strategy among the three tested strategies.
source: Among these, splitting the pegRNA at the repeat:anti-repeat portion is the most promising strategy, and can be potentially extended to the general gRNA used with CRISPR-Cas9 (Figure 1a, bottom; Figure 1b–e).

claim: The rates of prime editing using split pegRNA are strongly dependent on the complementarity between the repeat:anti-repeat region of crRNA and petracrRNA.
source: The resulting rates of prime editing are strongly dependent on the complementarity between the repeat:anti-repeat region of crRNA and petracrRNA.

claim: The split pegRNA design mimics the functional molecules within the native CRISPR-Cas9 system, initially discovered as the dual-RNA-guided system.

source: Among different RNA-protein pairs, we chose two pairs, MS2-MCP and BoxB-LambdaN (Katrekar et al., 2022; Legault et al., 1998; Salstrom and Szybalski, 1978), which can be used as adaptors for using protein-protein interactions to drive RNA-RNA interactions.

claim: Transfecting HEK293T cells with MCP-LambdaN, PE4max, crRNA-MS2, and BoxB-petracrRNA resulted in 15% editing efficiency, which was 52% of the editing rate achieved by standard epegRNA.
source: When we transfected HEK293T cells with plasmids expressing MCP-LambdaN, PE4max (Chen et al., 2021), crRNA-MS2, and BoxB-petracrRNA that target HEK3 locus and program for CTT insertion at +0 position, we observed 15% editing efficiency, which was 52% of the editing rate achieved by transfecting a single, standard epegRNA-expressing plasmid that programs the same edit along with the PE4max-expressing plasmid ('eCTT control') (Figure 2b).
evidence: The text describes experimental results shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Substituting the MCP-LambdaN-expression plasmid with a GFP-expressing filler plasmid reduced editing efficiency to 6% of the eCTT control.
source: When the MCP-LambdaN-expression plasmid was substituted with a GFP-expressing filler plasmid ('Filler GFP plasmid' condition in Figure 2b), editing efficiency dropped to 6% of the eCTT control, indicating that crRNA-MS2 and BoxB-petracrRNA can promote genome editing to a limited extent, presumably by forming an active pegRNA complex even without the additional dimerization domain.
evidence: The text describes experimental results shown in Figure 2b.

claim: crRNA-MS2 and BoxB-petracrRNA can promote genome editing to a limited extent even without the additional dimerization domain.
source: When the MCP-LambdaN-expression plasmid was substituted with a GFP-expressing filler plasmid ('Filler GFP plasmid' condition in Figure 2b), editing efficiency dropped to 6% of the eCTT control, indicating that crRNA-MS2 and BoxB-petracrRNA can promote genome editing to a limited extent, presumably by forming an active pegRNA complex even without the additional dimerization domain.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Both epitope-antibody/nanobody interactions (GCN4:scFv and ALFA-tag:NbALFA) were able to induce strong genome editing efficiencies, close to the levels observed with the MCP-LambdaN fusion protein.
source: First, we observe that both epitope-antibody/nanobody interactions were able to induce strong genome editing efficiencies, close to the levels observed with the MCP-LambdaN fusion protein (Figure 2b).

claim: Additional GCN4 epitopes in the 4xGCN4 design did not increase editing efficiency compared to 1xGCN4.
source: Interestingly, the additional GCN4 epitopes in the 4xGCN4 design did not seem to increase editing efficiency, possibly meaning either that GCN4:scFv binding is saturated and additional GCN4 epitopes do not make a difference in bringing crRNA and petracrRNA into proximity, or that only the scFv binding to one of GCN4 epitope contributes to the active pegRNA formation due to spatial constraints.

claim: Split-GFP designs generally have lower editing efficiency than epitope-antibody/nanobody interactions, possibly due to weaker interaction between GFP1-10 and GFP11.
source: Second, we observe that split-GFP designs generally have lower editing efficiency, possibly due to weaker interaction between GFP1-10 and GFP11 compared to epitope-antibody/nanobody interactions.

source: We also tested the split-GFP construct without a nuclear localization sequence, which resulted in an even lower editing efficiency, possibly indicating that the nuclear localization propensity of proteins tagged with the MCP or LambdaN could affect the effectiveness of P3 editing.
evidence: The text describes experimental results and provides a possible interpretation.

claim: Addition of 200 nM rapamycin to the FKBP-FRB pair resulted in 3.9-fold higher editing compared to no rapamycin condition (58% vs 15% normalized editing efficiency).
source: For example, we observed 3.9-fold higher editing upon the addition of 200 nM rapamycin to the FKBP-FRB pair compared to no rapamycin condition (58% vs 15% normalized editing efficiency), and 2.7-fold higher editing upon the addition of 100 μM ABA to the PYL-ABI pair compared to no ABA condition (36% vs 13% normalized editing efficiency) (Figure 2d).

claim: Addition of 100 μM ABA to the PYL-ABI pair resulted in 2.7-fold higher editing compared to no ABA condition (36% vs 13% normalized editing efficiency).
source: For example, we observed 3.9-fold higher editing upon the addition of 200 nM rapamycin to the FKBP-FRB pair compared to no rapamycin condition (58% vs 15% normalized editing efficiency), and 2.7-fold higher editing upon the addition of 100 μM ABA to the PYL-ABI pair compared to no ABA condition (36% vs 13% normalized editing efficiency) (Figure 2d).

claim: The efficiency of P3 editing increases with a higher number of G-C base-pairs and annealing length within the varied region of the repeat:anti-repeat duplex.

source: For all three base editors tested, we observe that the addition of LambdaN-MCP increases the editing efficiency (Figure 3c, left), although the change in the editing was greater for CBE4max (3.5-fold increase) and ABE8 (2.1-fold increase) than CBE2 (1.4-fold increase).

claim: The change in editing efficiency with LambdaN-MCP addition was greater for CBE4max (3.5-fold increase) and ABE8 (2.1-fold increase) than CBE2 (1.4-fold increase).
source: For all three base editors tested, we observe that the addition of LambdaN-MCP increases the editing efficiency (Figure 3c, left), although the change in the editing was greater for CBE4max (3.5-fold increase) and ABE8 (2.1-fold increase) than CBE2 (1.4-fold increase).
evidence: The text describes experimental results shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The observed differences in editing efficiency increase between base editors are possibly related to different endonuclease activity, as CBE2 uses deactivated Cas9 instead of Cas9 nickase.

claim: Combining RADARS with P3 editing resulted in normalized editing efficiency of 11.6 ± 0.7% with IL6 RNA, which was significantly higher than 8.2 ± 0.3% without IL6 RNA (p=0.005).

claim: Replacing ADAR-guide-RNA-LambdaN-PCP with ADAR-guide-RNA-GFP resulted in normalized editing efficiency of 5.5 ± 0.6%.
source: First, when we replace the plasmid expressing ADAR-guide-RNA-LambdaN-PCP with the ADAR-guide-RNA-GFP (with the cargo protein of GFP instead of LambdaN-PCP), we observe the normalized editing efficiency of 5.5 ± 0.6% (Figure 4d).

claim: crRNA-PP7 and BoxB-petracrRNA can induce 5.5% normalized editing efficiency without LambdaN-PCP in the system, characterizing the non-specific editing level of P3 editing.
source: This suggests that the crRNA-PP7 and BoxB-petracrRNA can induce 5.5% normalized editing efficiency without LambdaN-PCP in the system, characterizing the non-specific editing level of P3 editing, and suggesting that the remaining 2.7% of normalized editing efficiency background is due to non-specific editing of the RADARS system, possibly due to leaky expression of LambdaN-PCP even in the absence of IL6 target RNA.

claim: Replacing 50% of ADAR-guide-RNA-GFP expression plasmid with LambdaN-PCP expression plasmid increased normalized editing efficiency to 34 ± 1%.
source: Finally, when we replace 50% of ADAR-guide-RNA-GFP expression plasmid with LambdaN-PCP expression plasmid, we observe the normalized editing efficiency to increase up to 34 ± 1%, suggesting that the inclusion of the RNA-controlled protein expression module might be lowering the overall editing efficiency.

source: Finally, the current P3 editing design uses a pair of RNA aptamers and their corresponding protein binders, limiting the multiplex detection of protein-protein pairs.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the current approach.

claim: More orthogonal protein-RNA pairs need to be identified to allow for large numbers of P3 sensors for different protein-protein interactions to be deployed within the same cell.
source: More orthogonal protein-RNA pairs need to be identified e.g. using a massively parallel platform (Buenrostro et al., 2014) and/or computational prediction (Baek et al., 2024) to allow for large numbers of P3 sensors for different protein-protein interactions to be deployed within the same cell.
evidence: This is stated as a future direction with citation support.

claim: Overcoming four challenges (evaluating additional cellular contexts, improving efficiency and specificity, understanding the limit of detectable protein-protein interactions, and developing sensors compatible with multiplex P3 editing) is necessary for P3 editing to be broadly useful.
source: Overcoming these four challenges is necessary for P3 editing to be broadly useful for gating genome editing on physiological levels of specific protein-protein interactions in a multiplex fashion.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the challenges and future directions.
